primitives.name: Residual Skill Bias
primitives.verbatim_quote: The paper demonstrates that because high-volume elite finishers contribute disproportionately to training data, standard xG models systematically misprice those same players' shots — so GAX conflates "finishing ability" with "the model was fit on shots like yours." ## 2.

primitives.assumptions: High-volume players dominate training data; GAX reflects skill confounded by model training composition.
primitives.breakdown_regime: When shot volume exceeds 100 per season and positional priors are ignored.

reasoning_traces.think:
The core insight is that standard expected goals (xG) models exhibit systematic bias due to disproportionate representation of high-volume elite finishers in training data. This leads to a confounding of player skill with model training composition, manifesting in inflated goals-above-expected (GAX) scores for such players. The fundamental failure mode arises from the assumption that residuals reflect pure skill, when they actually reflect model misfit to the training distribution. The simulation framework in Davis and Robberechts (2024) evaluates this by varying true finishing skill multipliers α and shot volumes V, measuring detection rates of skilled players over 5 seasons. The key innovation lies in multi-calibration, which stratifies xG predictions by position and shot volume, thereby reducing the influence of training-data skew. This approach aligns with GSI’s need for calibrated uncertainty quantification and GSE’s requirement for robust state transitions in player efficiency modeling. The training contamination experiment serves as a stress test, injecting synthetic shots to observe how GAX shifts, confirming that model residuals are indeed biased by training composition rather than intrinsic skill.
